entries.1:1: Paul introduces himself as someone who belongs to Jesus and was chosen by God to announce the good news. It reminds the reader that God calls ordinary people to serve him with purpose.
entries.1:2: This good news wasn't a new idea; God had already promised it long ago through his prophets in the Scriptures. It shows God keeps his promises and plans ahead.
entries.1:3: The good news is about God's Son, who was born as a real human being from King David's family line. It means Jesus is genuinely one of us.
entries.1:4: The Holy Spirit proved Jesus is God's Son with power when God raised him from the dead. This gives the reader confidence that Jesus is who he claimed to be.
entries.1:5: Through Jesus we received God's kindness and were sent to help people of every nation trust and obey him. It means the message is for everyone, and we get to pass it on.
entries.1:6: The believers in Rome were among those God called to belong to Jesus. It reassures the reader that they too are personally chosen and included.
entries.1:7: Paul greets all the Christians in Rome as people God loves and has set apart for himself. It tells the reader they are loved and special to God, and wishes them grace and peace.
entries.1:8: Paul thanks God for the Roman believers because their faith is talked about everywhere. It encourages the reader that a genuine faith can inspire others far away.
entries.1:9: Paul calls God as a witness that he constantly remembers the Romans in his prayers. It shows how much he cares and models praying faithfully for others.
entries.1:10: Paul keeps praying that God will finally let him travel to Rome. It reminds the reader to keep bringing their plans to God and trust his timing.
entries.1:11: Paul longs to visit them so he can share something spiritual that will strengthen them. It shows that meeting together helps believers grow strong in faith.
entries.1:12: Paul says their time together will encourage both him and them through their shared faith. It reminds the reader that faith is mutual — we strengthen each other.
entries.1:13: Paul has often planned to visit so he can see some good results among them, just as he has among other peoples. It shows his desire to see real growth, not just talk.
entries.1:14: Paul feels a duty to share the good news with educated Greeks and with people of other nations, both wise and uneducated. It means nobody is too far or too different to hear about Jesus.
entries.1:15: Because of that duty, Paul is eager to preach the good news to the people in Rome too. It shows readiness to share faith wherever God places you.
entries.1:16: Paul isn't embarrassed about the good news because it carries God's power to save everyone who believes, starting with the Jews and then everyone else. It encourages the reader not to be ashamed of their faith.
entries.1:17: The good news shows how God makes people right with himself — through faith from start to finish. It means the reader doesn't earn it; they simply trust God and keep trusting.
entries.1:18: God's anger is revealed from heaven against all the wrong and evil people do, especially when they push the truth down to keep doing wrong. It warns the reader that ignoring truth has serious consequences.
entries.1:19: People can know about God because he has made it plain to them. It means no one can say they had no way of knowing God exists.
entries.1:20: Since the world was made, God's invisible qualities — his power and nature — can be clearly seen in what he created. It means creation itself points to God, so people have no excuse for ignoring him.
entries.1:21: Even though they knew about God, they didn't honour or thank him; instead their thinking became pointless and their hearts grew dark. It warns the reader to stay thankful and keep God first.
entries.1:22: They thought they were wise but actually became foolish. It reminds the reader that pride in your own cleverness can lead you far from the truth.
entries.1:23: They traded the glory of the eternal God for images of humans, birds, animals and reptiles. It shows how easily people replace the real God with things they can see and control.
entries.1:24: Because of this, God let them follow the evil desires of their hearts, leading to shameful treatment of one another. It shows that rejecting God can lead to harmful choices.
entries.1:25: They swapped God's truth for a lie and worshipped created things instead of the Creator. It warns the reader against putting anything in the place that belongs to God.
entries.1:26: Because of this, God handed them over to shameful desires, with women turning from natural relations to unnatural ones. It describes the consequences of turning away from God's design.
entries.1:27: In the same way, men left natural relations with women and burned with desire for each other, receiving the due penalty for their error. It shows that wrong desires carry real consequences.
entries.1:28: Since they didn't think it worthwhile to keep God in their knowledge, God let them go to a worthless mind, doing what is not right. It warns the reader to keep God central in their thinking.
entries.1:29: They became full of every kind of wrong — greed, hatred, envy, murder, fighting, deceit, gossip and slander. It shows how far a heart can drift when God is left out.
entries.1:30: They became proud, boastful, disrespectful, inventors of evil, and disobedient to parents. It reminds the reader that these attitudes are serious, not small flaws.
entries.1:31: They became senseless, unfaithful to their promises, unloving and unmerciful. It shows the kind of character that develops without God, and calls the reader toward the opposite.
entries.1:32: They know God's law says such things deserve death, yet they keep doing them and approve of others who do. It warns the reader that approving of wrong is just as serious as doing it.
entries.2:1: Paul says that when we judge others for things we also do, we are really condemning ourselves. It means we should look honestly at our own faults before pointing out someone else's.
entries.2:2: God judges people who do wrong fairly and truly. It means God sees clearly what people do and his judgment can be trusted.
entries.2:3: It makes no sense to judge others for what we ourselves do and still expect to escape God's judgment. It means we can't fool God by pointing at others while ignoring our own wrong.
entries.2:4: God has been patient and kind with us, waiting for us to change, and that kindness is meant to lead us to turn from wrong. It means we shouldn't treat God's patience as if it doesn't matter.
entries.2:5: If we refuse to change and stay stubborn, we are piling up judgment for ourselves instead of mercy. It means a hard heart stores up trouble for the day God judges rightly.
entries.2:6: God will give each person exactly what their life deserves. It means our actions really matter to God and nothing is overlooked.
entries.2:7: People who keep doing good and seek God's glory and honor will receive eternal life. It means steady, patient goodness is what God rewards with life that never ends.
entries.2:8: People who are selfish and push away the truth will face God's anger. It means choosing self and rejecting truth leads to serious consequences.
entries.2:9: Trouble and distress come to everyone who does evil, whether Jew or non-Jew. It means no one escapes the results of wrongdoing, whatever their background.
entries.2:10: Glory, honor, and peace come to everyone who does good, whether Jew or non-Jew. It means God blesses good living equally, regardless of who you are.
entries.2:11: God does not play favorites with anyone. It means we can't expect special treatment from God because of our background or status.
entries.2:12: People who sin without knowing God's law will be judged apart from it, and those who sin under the law will be judged by it. It means everyone is accountable to God in the way they were given.
entries.2:13: Just hearing God's law doesn't make a person right with God; only doing it does. It means knowing what's right counts for nothing unless we actually live it.
entries.2:14: People without God's written law who naturally do what it says show they have a kind of law inside them. It means right and wrong can be known even without the rulebook.
entries.2:15: Their conscience shows the law's work written on their hearts, sometimes accusing and sometimes approving them. It means God has built a sense of right and wrong into every person.
entries.2:16: On the day God judges people's hidden secrets through Jesus Christ, this inner witness will matter. It means nothing hidden stays hidden, and Jesus is the one through whom God judges.
entries.2:17: Paul turns to those who call themselves Jews, rely on the law, and boast about knowing God. It means religious identity and knowledge alone are not enough.
entries.2:18: They know what God wants and can tell right from wrong because they've been taught the law. It means knowing God's will is a privilege that comes with responsibility.
entries.2:19: They see themselves as guides for the blind and lights for those in darkness. It means it's easy to think of yourself as the expert who helps others.
entries.2:20: They consider themselves teachers of the foolish, holding the very shape of knowledge and truth in the law. It means having the truth can make a person feel superior to others.
entries.2:21: Paul asks whether those who teach others also teach themselves, and whether those who forbid stealing actually steal. It means we should practice what we preach.
entries.2:22: He asks whether those who condemn adultery commit it themselves, and whether those who hate idols rob temples. It means it's easy to condemn in others what we quietly do ourselves.
entries.2:23: Boasting in the law while breaking it dishonors God. It means religious pride paired with disobedience actually brings shame to God's name.
entries.2:24: Because of such behavior, God's name is spoken of badly among outsiders, just as the Scriptures say. It means our hypocrisy can make God look bad to those watching.
entries.2:25: Circumcision is valuable only if you keep the law; if you break it, it's as if you were never circumcised. It means the outward sign means nothing without real obedience.
entries.2:26: If uncircumcised people keep the law's requirements, won't they be counted as circumcised? It means God values obedience over outward religious markers.
entries.2:27: Those who keep the law without the outward sign will stand as a witness against you who have the sign but break the law. It means outward religion without obedience is exposed.
entries.2:28: Being a real Jew isn't just about outward appearance, and real circumcision isn't just physical. It means God looks past external labels to what's inside.
entries.2:29: A true Jew is one inwardly, circumcised in the heart by the Spirit, not by written rules, and praised by God rather than people. It means God cares about a changed heart, not outward approval.
entries.3:1: Paul asks whether being Jewish or circumcised gives someone an advantage. He is setting up to answer his own question, not denying that it mattered.
entries.3:2: Yes, there was a big advantage: God trusted the Jewish people with his own words. Being given God's message is a real privilege.
entries.3:3: Some of them did not believe, but that does not cancel God's faithfulness. People's unfaithfulness does not make God unreliable.
entries.3:4: God is always true even when every person proves false. When God is judged, he comes out right, and his words stand.
entries.3:5: If our wrong makes God's rightness look better, is God unfair to punish us? Paul raises the question people might ask.
entries.3:6: Absolutely not. If God were unfair, he could not be the judge of the whole world.
entries.3:7: If my lie makes God's truth shine brighter, why am I still treated as a sinner? Paul voices the objection people raise.
entries.3:8: Some accused Paul of teaching that we should do evil so good can come. He says that idea is false and those who do it deserve judgment.
entries.3:9: So are Jews better off? No. Paul has already shown that Jews and non-Jews alike are all trapped under sin.
entries.3:10: Paul quotes Scripture to back this up: no one is righteous, not even one person.
entries.3:11: No one truly understands or seeks after God on their own. Left to ourselves, we do not look for him.
entries.3:12: Everyone has turned away and become useless for good. No one does good, not a single person.
entries.3:13: Their speech is corrupt and deadly, full of lies and poison. Words reveal what is inside.
entries.3:14: Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness. The way they talk shows a heart far from God.
entries.3:15: They are quick to run toward violence and bloodshed. Harming others comes easily to them.
entries.3:16: Wherever they go they leave ruin and misery behind. Their path causes damage.
entries.3:17: They do not know the way of peace. They have no real experience of living in peace with God or others.
entries.3:18: They live without any fear of God before their eyes. Reverence for God is completely missing.
entries.3:19: The law speaks to those under it, so that no one can talk back and the whole world stands accountable to God.
entries.3:20: Keeping the law cannot make anyone right with God. The law's real job is to show us our sin.
entries.3:21: But now God has shown a way to be right with him apart from law-keeping, and the Law and Prophets already pointed to it.
entries.3:22: This right standing comes through faith in Jesus Christ to everyone who believes. There is no difference between people.
entries.3:23: Everyone has sinned and falls short of God's glory. No one measures up on their own.
entries.3:24: Yet people are made right with God freely, as a gift of his grace, through the rescue that is in Christ Jesus.
entries.3:25: God presented Jesus as the place where mercy meets us, received by faith through his blood. This shows God's justice in passing over earlier sins.
entries.3:26: God did this to show his justice now, proving he is right and that he makes right those who trust in Jesus.
entries.3:27: So there is no room to boast. Boasting is ruled out—not by a rule of works, but by a rule of faith.
entries.3:28: We conclude that a person is made right with God by faith, apart from doing the works of the law.
entries.3:29: Is God only the God of Jews? No, he is also the God of non-Jews.
entries.3:30: Since God is one, he makes both circumcised and uncircumcised right with himself on the same basis: faith.
entries.3:31: Does faith cancel the law? Not at all. Faith actually upholds the law and shows its true importance.
entries.4:1: Paul asks what Abraham, the ancestor of the Jewish people, actually gained from his relationship with God. It invites the reader to look at Abraham's example and see what really counted.
entries.4:2: If Abraham had earned God's approval by his own good deeds, he could brag about it. But he had nothing to boast about in God's presence, so his acceptance must have come another way.
entries.4:3: Scripture says Abraham simply trusted God, and God counted that trust as righteousness. It means being right with God starts with believing him, not with earning it.
entries.4:4: When someone works for a wage, the payment is owed to them, not given as a gift. So if righteousness were earned, it would be a debt God owes rather than kindness.
entries.4:5: The person who stops trying to earn it and simply trusts God, who accepts even wrongdoers, is credited with righteousness. That means you can come to God as you are, trusting him rather than your record.
entries.4:6: David is cited as saying the same thing: there is real blessing for the person God counts as righteous apart from their works. It shows this isn't a new idea but runs through Scripture.
entries.4:7: David calls people happy whose wrongs are forgiven and whose sins are covered over. The point for the reader is that forgiveness brings genuine joy and relief.
entries.4:8: The person is blessed whom the Lord does not hold their sin against. It means God's forgiveness is real and complete, not a partial settling of accounts.
entries.4:9: Paul asks whether this blessing is only for the circumcised Jews or also for uncircumcised outsiders. Since Abraham's faith was credited before any ritual, the blessing is open to everyone.
entries.4:10: The key question is when Abraham was counted righteous—before or after he was circumcised. It happened before, which shows the ritual wasn't what made him right with God.
entries.4:11: Circumcision was later given as a sign and seal of the faith he already had. So Abraham becomes the spiritual father of all who believe, even without that ritual, so their faith is credited too.
entries.4:12: Abraham is also father of the circumcised—but only of those who follow the same path of faith he had before his circumcision. It means heritage and ritual alone don't count; walking in faith does.
entries.4:13: God's promise that Abraham would inherit the world came through the righteousness of faith, not through keeping the law. The promise rests on trust, not on rule-keeping.
entries.4:14: If only law-keepers got the inheritance, then faith would be pointless and God's promise would be empty. Trusting God would mean nothing if earning it were the real requirement.
entries.4:15: The law produces wrath because it exposes and punishes wrongdoing. Where there is no law, there is no violation to be charged—so the law can't be the path to the promise.
entries.4:16: That's why the promise comes by faith, so it can be a free gift guaranteed to all Abraham's descendants—both law-keepers and those who share his faith. Grace, not performance, makes the promise sure.
entries.4:17: Scripture calls Abraham the father of many nations, and he believed the God who raises the dead and calls into being what does not exist. The reader is asked to trust that same kind of God.
entries.4:18: Abraham hoped even when there was no human reason to hope, believing God's promise of countless descendants. Faith keeps hoping because it rests on God's word, not on circumstances.
entries.4:19: Abraham's body was as good as dead at about a hundred, and Sarah could no longer have children, yet his faith didn't weaken. Age and impossibility didn't stop him from trusting.
entries.4:20: He didn't waver in unbelief about God's promise but grew strong in faith and gave God glory. Trusting God's promise honors him, even when the odds look bad.
entries.4:21: Abraham was fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised. That kind of confidence in God's reliability is what faith looks like.
entries.4:22: Because Abraham believed, God counted it to him as righteousness. Trusting God's promise is what put him right with God.
entries.4:23: The record of Abraham's faith being credited wasn't written for his sake alone. It was preserved so later readers would learn from his example.
entries.4:24: It was written for us too, who will have righteousness credited to us if we trust the God who raised Jesus from the dead. The same faith that worked for Abraham is available to the reader.
entries.4:25: Jesus was handed over to death because of our wrongdoing and raised to life so we could be made right with God. His death and resurrection are the ground on which our forgiveness and righteousness rest.
entries.5:1: Because faith has made us right with God, we can now live at peace with him, and Jesus is the one who made that possible. For you, this means you don't have to feel God is against you anymore.
entries.5:2: Through Jesus we have gained access by faith to this grace we now stand in, and we can be glad as we look forward to sharing God's glory. For you, this means your standing with God is secure and your future is bright.
entries.5:3: We can even be glad in our troubles, because trouble teaches us to keep waiting patiently. For you, this means hard times are not wasted; they build something good in you.
entries.5:4: Patient waiting builds proven character, and proven character builds hope. For you, this means the endurance you learn now gives you solid confidence for what's ahead.
entries.5:5: That hope won't leave us disappointed, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit he gave us. For you, this means you can trust your hope because God's love is real inside you.
entries.5:6: When we were powerless to help ourselves, at just the right time Christ died for people who were doing wrong. For you, this means God acted for you when you couldn't act for yourself.
entries.5:7: It's rare for anyone to die even for a good person, though someone might possibly die for a truly good man. For you, this shows how unusual and costly real sacrifice is.
entries.5:8: God loved us before we were worth loving. Grace is not a reward for good behaviour.
entries.5:9: Since we are now made right with God by Christ's blood, we can be even more certain we'll be saved from God's judgment through him. For you, this means your rescue is secure, not shaky.
entries.5:10: If God made peace with us through his Son's death while we were still his enemies, then now that we are his friends we will surely be saved through his life. For you, this means Jesus' living presence keeps you safe.
entries.5:11: More than that, we can celebrate God himself through Jesus, who has brought us into peace with God. For you, this means your joy can be in God himself, not just in what he gives.
entries.5:12: Sin entered the world through one man, and death came with sin, so death spread to everyone because everyone has done wrong. For you, this explains why the world is broken and why we all need help.
entries.5:13: Sin was already in the world before the law was given, but sin isn't counted against anyone when there's no law to break. For you, this means wrongdoing existed long before rules named it.
entries.5:14: Even so, death ruled from Adam to Moses, even over people whose sin wasn't like Adam's. Adam points ahead to the one who was coming. For you, this means Adam's story sets up the greater story of Christ.
entries.5:15: God's free gift is not like Adam's failure. If one man's wrong brought death to many, God's grace and the gift through one man, Jesus Christ, overflow to many. For you, this means grace is far bigger than the damage sin caused.
entries.5:16: The gift isn't like the result of that one sin. One sin brought a guilty verdict, but the free gift brings being made right with God despite many wrongs. For you, this means God's gift does more than just cancel one mistake.
entries.5:17: If death ruled through one man's wrong, how much more will those who receive God's abundant grace and the gift of righteousness rule in life through Jesus Christ. For you, this means grace puts you on top of what once ruled you.
entries.5:18: Just as one wrong act brought judgment on all people, so one right act brings a right standing that leads to life for all. For you, this means Jesus' one act opened the door to life.
entries.5:19: Just as many became sinners through one man's disobedience, so many will be made righteous through one man's obedience. For you, this means Jesus' faithfulness undoes what Adam's failure started.
entries.5:20: The law came in so that wrongdoing would become even more obvious, but where sin increased, grace increased far more. For you, this means no amount of sin outruns God's grace.
entries.5:21: Sin once ruled through death, but now grace rules through righteousness, leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. For you, this means grace, not sin, gets the final word in your life.
entries.6:1: Paul asks whether we should keep sinning so that God's grace can show even more. It means grace is not an excuse to sin, so the reader should not treat God's kindness as permission to do wrong.
entries.6:2: Paul firmly says no, because a person who has truly turned from sin cannot keep living in it. It means your new life with God should change how you live, not leave you the same.
entries.6:3: Paul reminds them that being baptized into Christ means being joined to his death. It means your baptism pictured leaving your old life behind with Jesus.
entries.6:4: Baptism pictured being buried with Christ, and just as the Father raised him, we are meant to live a new kind of life. It means your life should show the fresh start God has given you.
entries.6:5: If we have been joined to Christ in a death like his, we will also be joined to him in a resurrection like his. It means the same power that raised Jesus will raise us too.
entries.6:6: Our old self was nailed to the cross with Christ so that sin's grip on us could be broken and we would no longer be slaves to sin. It means you are not chained to your old habits anymore.
entries.6:7: A person who has died is no longer under sin's claim. It means death to the old life breaks sin's hold on you.
entries.6:8: If we died with Christ, we trust that we will also live with him. It means your future with Christ is secure because you belong to him.
entries.6:9: Christ rose from the dead and will never die again, because death has no power over him anymore. It means Jesus' victory over death is permanent and cannot be undone.
entries.6:10: Jesus died once to deal with sin and now lives fully for God. It means his work is finished, and his life now is completely devoted to God.
entries.6:11: Paul tells believers to count themselves as dead to sin but alive to God in Christ. It means you should see yourself the way God sees you and live that way.
entries.6:12: Don't let sin rule your body or make you obey its cravings. It means you can say no to sinful desires instead of letting them control you.
entries.6:13: Don't hand your body over to sin as a tool for evil; instead give yourself to God as someone brought from death to life. It means use your whole self for good, not for wrong.
entries.6:14: Sin will not master you, because you are not under law but under grace. It means God's grace gives you power to overcome sin rather than being trapped by it.
entries.6:15: Paul asks again whether grace means we can keep sinning, and answers no. It means being forgiven does not make sin acceptable.
entries.6:16: You become a servant of whatever you give yourself to obey, whether sin leading to death or God leading to righteousness. It means choose carefully what you let control your life.
entries.6:17: Paul thanks God that although they once were slaves to sin, they wholeheartedly obeyed the teaching they received. It means turning to God's truth changes your direction.
entries.6:18: Now that sin no longer rules them, they have become servants of what is right. It means freedom from sin means belonging to God and doing good.
entries.6:19: Paul uses everyday language because they are still growing; just as they once gave themselves to impurity, now they should give themselves to righteousness. It means put the same energy into doing good that you once put into wrong.
entries.6:20: When they were slaves to sin, they had nothing to do with righteousness. It means sin and doing right cannot both run your life.
entries.6:21: Paul asks what good came from the things they are now ashamed of, since those things end in death. It means sin gives no lasting benefit, only regret and loss.
entries.6:22: Now that they are free from sin and serve God, their lives produce holy fruit and end in eternal life. It means serving God brings real and lasting good.
entries.6:23: Sin pays death; God gives life through Jesus. Two wages, one choice.
entries.7:1: Paul reminds Jewish believers that a law only has authority over someone while that person is alive. This means death ends a person's obligation to the law.
entries.7:2: A married woman is legally bound to her husband only while he lives; if he dies, that bond no longer applies to her. The point is that death breaks a legal obligation.
entries.7:3: If she takes another man while her husband is alive, she is called an adulteress, but after his death she is free and not guilty. Death releases a person from that legal tie.
entries.7:4: In the same way, through Christ's body you died to the law, so you could belong to the risen Christ and produce good fruit for God. Your old legal bond is over, and your life now belongs to him.
entries.7:5: When we lived by our sinful nature, the law stirred up wrong desires that worked in us and produced death. Being ruled by those desires only led to ruin.
entries.7:6: Now we are released from the law, having died to what held us, so we serve God in a new way by the Spirit, not the old way of written rules. Our service to God is now inward and alive, not just outward rule-keeping.
entries.7:7: The law itself is not sin; it showed Paul what sin is, since he would not have known coveting was wrong without the command against it. The law reveals sin rather than causing it.
entries.7:8: Sin used the command as an opportunity to stir up all kinds of wrong desires in him, because without law sin has no life. The command exposed and provoked the sin that was already there.
entries.7:9: There was a time Paul lived without the law, but when the command came, sin came alive and he died. The law made him realize he was guilty and under judgment.
entries.7:10: The command meant to bring life turned out to bring death for him. What was good in itself exposed his failure and brought condemnation.
entries.7:11: Sin deceived him and used the command to put him to death. Sin twists even good commands to trap people.
entries.7:12: The law is holy, and its commands are holy, right, and good. The problem is never the law itself; it is trustworthy and good.
entries.7:13: The good law did not cause his death; rather, sin used something good to bring death, so sin would be exposed as truly sinful. The law shows how bad sin really is.
entries.7:14: The law is spiritual, but Paul describes himself as fleshly, sold under sin. He admits he is weak and captive to sin apart from God's help.
entries.7:15: He does not understand his own actions, because he does not do what he wants and instead does what he hates. This is the common struggle of wanting good but doing wrong.
entries.7:16: If he does what he does not want to do, he agrees that the law is good. His failure actually confirms the law is right.
entries.7:17: So it is no longer he himself doing it, but sin living in him. He distinguishes his real desire from the sin that pushes him.
entries.7:18: He knows nothing good lives in his sinful nature; he has the desire to do right but not the power. Wanting good is not enough without God's strength.
entries.7:19: He does not do the good he wants, but he does the evil he does not want. This describes the frustrating gap between intention and action.
entries.7:20: If he does what he does not want, then it is sin living in him doing it, not his true self. The sin inside him is the real culprit.
entries.7:21: He finds this pattern: when he wants to do good, evil is right there with him. Doing right is a real struggle because evil is always present.
entries.7:22: In his inner being he delights in God's law. His deepest self actually loves what God commands.
entries.7:23: But he sees another law in his body fighting against his mind and making him a prisoner to sin. His body pulls against his good intentions.
entries.7:24: He cries out as a miserable person, asking who will rescue him from this body of death. He longs for rescue from the sin that drags him down.
entries.7:25: He thanks God that rescue comes through Jesus Christ, then sums up the struggle: his mind serves God's law but his flesh serves sin's law. The answer to his cry is Jesus, even while the battle continues.
entries.8:1: There is now no condemnation for those in Christ. The verdict has already been settled.
entries.8:2: The Spirit of God, working through Jesus, sets you free from the cycle of sin and death. You no longer have to live as a slave to that old pattern.
entries.8:3: The law couldn't fix us because our human weakness got in the way, so God sent his own Son in a human body to deal with sin. God passed judgment on sin in human flesh, doing what the law couldn't.
entries.8:4: The righteous requirement of the law can now be fulfilled in us who live by the Spirit rather than by our sinful nature. God's standard is met in us as we follow the Spirit.
entries.8:5: People controlled by their sinful nature focus their minds on selfish things, while those who live by the Spirit focus on what the Spirit wants. Your mindset reveals which direction your life is headed.
entries.8:6: A mind set on selfish desires leads to death, but a mind set on the Spirit brings life and peace. What you focus your thoughts on shapes your whole life.
entries.8:7: A mind controlled by the sinful nature is hostile toward God and can't submit to him. Such a mindset is fundamentally at odds with God's will.
entries.8:8: Those who live according to their sinful nature cannot please God. If you want to please God, you must live by his Spirit.
entries.8:9: You are not controlled by the sinful nature but by the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in you. Anyone who doesn't have the Spirit of Christ doesn't belong to him.
entries.8:10: If Christ is in you, your body is still subject to death because of sin, but the Spirit gives you life because of righteousness. Your spiritual life is secure even though your body will die.
entries.8:11: The same Spirit that raised Jesus from the dead lives in you and will also give life to your mortal body. God's resurrection power is at work in you right now.
entries.8:12: We have an obligation, but not to our sinful nature to live according to it. We owe our lives to the Spirit, not to our old selfish desires.
entries.8:13: If you live according to the sinful nature, you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the misdeeds of the body, you will live. You must actively say no to sin with the Spirit's help.
entries.8:14: Those who are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God. Being God's child means following the Spirit's guidance.
entries.8:15: You didn't receive a spirit of fear and slavery again, but a spirit of adoption as sons and daughters, by which we cry out to God as Father. You can approach God with confidence as his child, not with fear.
entries.8:16: The Spirit himself confirms to our spirit that we are God's children. God's Spirit gives you inner assurance that you truly belong to him.
entries.8:17: If we are God's children, we are also heirs, sharing in God's inheritance together with Christ. If we share in Christ's sufferings, we will also share in his glory.
entries.8:18: The sufferings of this present life are not worth comparing to the glory that will be revealed in us. Whatever pain you face now is temporary compared to the future God has for you.
entries.8:19: All of creation eagerly waits for God's children to be revealed. The whole world is longing for the day when God's family is fully shown.
entries.8:20: Creation was subjected to frustration, not by its own choice but by God's will, yet with hope. Even the brokenness of the world carries the promise of something better.
entries.8:21: Creation itself will be freed from its bondage to decay and share in the freedom and glory of God's children. The whole world will one day be restored.
entries.8:22: We know that all creation has been groaning in pain up to this present time. The world around us is suffering and waiting for relief.
entries.8:23: We who have the firstfruits of the Spirit also groan inwardly, waiting for our adoption and the redemption of our bodies. Even believers feel the ache of waiting for God's full work to be completed.
entries.8:24: Our salvation is something we hope for, but hope that is already seen isn't really hope. You are saved in a way that still requires trusting in what you can't yet see.
entries.8:25: If we hope for what we don't yet see, we wait for it patiently. Trusting God means holding on with patience while you wait for his promises.
entries.8:26: The Spirit helps us in our weakness, because we don't know how to pray properly, and the Spirit intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. When you don't know what to pray, the Spirit prays for you.
entries.8:27: God, who searches our hearts, knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for God's people according to God's will. Your prayers are heard and aligned with God's purposes through the Spirit.
entries.8:28: God works everything together for good for those who love him. Not that everything is good, but that nothing is wasted.
entries.8:29: Those God knew beforehand he also predestined to be conformed to the likeness of his Son, so that Christ might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters. God's plan is to shape you into the image of Jesus.
entries.8:30: Those God predestined he also called, those he called he also justified, and those he justified he also glorified. God's work in your life is a complete chain from beginning to end.
entries.8:31: If God is on your side, the opposition loses its case. You are not alone in the argument.
entries.8:32: God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, so he will surely also freely give us all things. If God gave the greatest gift, you can trust him for everything else.
entries.8:33: Who can bring any charge against God's chosen people? It is God himself who justifies. No accusation against you stands, because God himself declares you not guilty.
entries.8:34: Who can condemn you? Christ Jesus died, was raised, and is at God's right hand interceding for us. Jesus himself is on your side, speaking up for you.
entries.8:35: Who can separate us from the love of Christ? Trouble, hardship, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, or sword cannot. Nothing you face can cut you off from Christ's love.
entries.8:36: As Scripture says, we face death all day long for your sake and are considered sheep to be slaughtered. Following God can mean real suffering, just as Scripture describes.
entries.8:37: In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. Through Christ's love, you don't just survive hardship—you overcome it.
entries.8:38: I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor rulers, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers can separate us. Nothing in all of existence has the power to break God's love for you.
entries.8:39: Nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. No height, depth, or created thing can come between you and God's love.
entries.9:1: Paul is swearing that he is telling the truth, and his own conscience, guided by the Holy Spirit, confirms it. He wants his readers to trust that what follows comes from sincere conviction.
entries.9:2: Paul feels deep, unending grief. He is genuinely heartbroken, not exaggerating, and wants readers to see how much he cares.
entries.9:3: Paul is so devoted to his fellow Jews that he would be willing to be cut off from Christ if it could save them. This shows how far love for others can go.
entries.9:4: The Israelites were given enormous privileges: adoption as God's children, God's glory, covenants, the law, worship, and promises. These were real gifts from God, not something earned.
entries.9:5: The great ancestors belong to Israel, and even Christ came from them in his human family line. Yet Christ is God over all, worthy of eternal praise.
entries.9:6: God's promises did not fail just because many Israelites rejected Christ. Being physically descended from Israel does not automatically make someone part of God's true people.
entries.9:7: Mere descent from Abraham does not make someone a child of the promise. God told Abraham that his line would be traced through Isaac specifically, not through every descendant.
entries.9:8: God's children are not defined by physical ancestry but by God's own promise. It is God's initiative, not human bloodline, that makes someone part of his family.
entries.9:9: God's promise was concrete: at a set time he would return, and Sarah would have a son. The promise depended on God acting, not on human effort.
entries.9:10: Paul adds another example: Rebecca became pregnant by Isaac with twin sons. This sets up a case where God's choice was made before either child was born.
entries.9:11: Before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, God's purpose was already set. His choice was based on his own plan, not on anyone's deeds.
entries.9:12: God told Rebecca that the older son would serve the younger. This reversed the normal custom, showing God's choice was his own to make.
entries.9:13: God loved Jacob and rejected Esau. This is strong language showing that God's choice is real and not based on human merit.
entries.9:14: Someone might object that God is unfair. Paul firmly rejects that idea: God is not unjust in making his choices.
entries.9:15: God told Moses that he shows mercy and compassion to whomever he chooses. Mercy is God's to give freely, not something anyone can demand.
entries.9:16: Getting God's mercy does not depend on what a person wants or works for. It depends on God, who shows mercy.
entries.9:17: God told Pharaoh that he had been raised up so God's power could be displayed through him and God's name proclaimed worldwide. Even a resistant ruler served God's larger purpose.
entries.9:18: God is free to show mercy to whom he will and to let others become hard-hearted. This is his prerogative, not something humans control.
entries.9:19: A natural objection follows: if God decides these things, why does he still blame people? Who can resist his plan? Paul raises this question to address it.
entries.9:20: Paul answers that a human being has no right to argue with God. A created thing cannot demand explanations from the one who made it.
entries.9:21: A potter can make different vessels from the same clay, some for honorable use and some for ordinary use. The maker has the right to decide.
entries.9:22: God patiently endured people who were objects of his wrath and headed for destruction, wanting to show his anger and power. His patience is real, even toward those who resist him.
entries.9:23: God also wanted to display the richness of his glory to people who received mercy and were prepared for glory. His mercy is meant to be seen and praised.
entries.9:24: These people whom God called include not only Jews but also non-Jews. God's call reaches beyond one nation.
entries.9:25: God said through Hosea that people who were not his people would be called his people, and one who was not loved would be loved. God can bring outsiders into his family.
entries.9:26: In the very place where they were told they were not God's people, they will be called children of the living God. God can transform rejection into adoption.
entries.9:27: Isaiah said that even if Israel's numbers were as vast as sand on the seashore, only a remnant would be saved. Large numbers do not guarantee salvation.
entries.9:28: The Lord will carry out his word on earth quickly and decisively. His judgment is thorough and will not be delayed forever.
entries.9:29: Isaiah said that unless the Lord of hosts had left them some offspring, Israel would have been wiped out like Sodom and Gomorrah. God's mercy preserved a remnant.
entries.9:30: Non-Jews who were not even pursuing righteousness obtained it, and they got it through faith. Right standing with God comes by trusting him, not by chasing it through rules.
entries.9:31: Israel pursued a law meant to produce righteousness but did not reach it. Effort alone did not get them there.
entries.9:32: They missed it because they sought it by works rather than by faith. They stumbled over the stone in their path, which is Christ.
entries.9:33: God placed in Zion a stone that causes stumbling, yet whoever believes in him will not be disappointed. Trusting Christ is the safe path; rejecting him is the stumbling block.
entries.10:1: Paul deeply wants his fellow Jews to be saved, and he prays for it. It shows that caring about people's salvation should move us to pray for them.
entries.10:2: The people Paul is talking about are sincere and eager about God, but their zeal is not guided by truly knowing him. Sincerity alone isn't enough; we need to know God as he really is.
entries.10:3: They didn't understand the righteousness God gives, so they tried to build their own instead of accepting God's. We can make the same mistake by trusting our own efforts rather than God's gift.
entries.10:4: Christ fulfills the purpose of the law, so that everyone who believes can be made right with God. Faith in Jesus, not law-keeping, is the way to righteousness.
entries.10:5: Moses taught that keeping the law perfectly would bring life, but that requires complete obedience. It shows that the law's way demands what we cannot do on our own.
entries.10:6: Faith's righteousness doesn't require some impossible feat, like going up to heaven to bring Christ down. You don't have to do something spectacular to be saved.
entries.10:7: Nor does it require going down into the depths to bring Christ back from the dead. God has already done the hard part; we don't need to.
entries.10:8: The message of faith is close and accessible, right there in your mouth and heart. You don't have to search far; the good news is near you and can be believed and spoken.
entries.10:9: Believe in your heart and say it with your mouth. Faith is not meant to stay secret.
entries.10:10: Believing in your heart makes you right with God, and openly confessing Jesus as Lord brings salvation. Faith is inward, but it also shows itself in what we say.
entries.10:11: Scripture promises that no one who trusts in him will be put to shame. You can rely on him without fear of being let down.
entries.10:12: There is no difference between Jew and non-Jew, because the same Lord is over all and generous to everyone who calls on him. God's welcome is open to all people equally.
entries.10:13: Everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved. Salvation is available to anyone who turns to him, no matter who they are.
entries.10:14: People can't call on someone they don't believe in, believe without hearing, or hear without someone telling them. This is why sharing the message with others matters.
entries.10:15: Preachers must be sent, and Scripture calls beautiful the feet of those who bring good news. Those who carry the message to others are doing something truly valuable.
entries.10:16: Not everyone who hears the good news accepts it, as Isaiah's question shows. Hearing alone isn't enough; the message must be believed.
entries.10:17: Faith comes from hearing the message, and that message is about Christ. If you want faith to grow, keep listening to what God says about Jesus.
entries.10:18: The message did reach them; it has gone out across the earth. No one can claim they never had the chance to hear.
entries.10:19: Israel did have knowledge, yet God warned through Moses that he would make them jealous by reaching other peoples. God's blessing to outsiders is a wake-up call to those who ignore him.
entries.10:20: Isaiah boldly says that people who weren't looking for God found him, and he showed himself to those who weren't seeking him. God often reaches people we wouldn't expect.
entries.10:21: Yet about Israel God says he kept reaching out all day to a stubborn people who resisted him. God is patient and keeps offering himself even to those who turn away.
entries.11:1: Paul insists God has not rejected the Jewish people, and he points to himself—a Jew from Abraham's line—as living proof. God's promises to his people still stand, so no reader should assume he has abandoned them.
entries.11:2: God has not thrown away the people he chose, and Paul reminds readers that even Elijah once complained to God about Israel. God's commitment to his chosen people is steady, even when things look bad.
entries.11:3: Elijah felt totally alone, telling God that the people had killed the prophets and were hunting him down. It's a picture of someone convinced that faithfulness has failed and no one else is left.
entries.11:4: God corrected Elijah, saying he still had seven thousand people who had never bowed to the false god Baal. God's work is often bigger than the lonely person can see.
entries.11:5: Just as in Elijah's day, God still has a group of people chosen by his free kindness. Being part of God's people is a gift of grace, not something earned.
entries.11:6: If being chosen is a gift of grace, then it can't be based on good works—otherwise grace wouldn't be grace at all. Readers should rest in God's free gift rather than trying to earn it.
entries.11:7: Israel as a whole didn't find what it was looking for, but the chosen ones did, while the rest became hardened. The difference comes down to God's selection, not human effort.
entries.11:8: Scripture describes God giving these people a kind of spiritual sleep, so they couldn't see or hear the truth. It's a sober warning that hearts can become dull to God.
entries.11:9: David describes their own table—their blessings and comforts—becoming a trap and a stumbling block to them. Good things can become snares when the heart is wrong.
entries.11:10: Their eyes are darkened so they can't see, and their backs are bent under a burden. This pictures the sad condition of those who have turned away from God.
entries.11:11: Their stumbling was not the end of the story—God used it to bring salvation to non-Jews, hoping to stir Israel to want what others received. God turns failure into an opening for blessing.
entries.11:12: If their failure brought such wealth to the world, their full restoration will be far greater still. God's plans only get bigger and better, so readers can hope.
entries.11:13: Paul speaks directly to non-Jewish believers and takes his role as their apostle seriously. He wants them to see that God has a purpose for them too.
entries.11:14: Paul hopes his work among non-Jews will make his own people jealous and bring some of them to salvation. Love for his own people drives his mission.
entries.11:15: If their rejection brought the world into friendship with God, their welcome back will be like life from the dead. God's mercy toward them will be a stunning revival.
entries.11:16: If the first part of the dough is holy, the whole batch is holy, and if the root is holy, so are the branches. God's set-apart beginning means the whole people still belongs to him.
entries.11:17: Some branches were broken off, and non-Jewish believers—like a wild olive branch—were grafted in to share the rich life of the root. Readers who were outsiders now share in God's blessing.
entries.11:18: Don't look down on the branches that were removed, because the root supports you—not the other way around. Pride has no place for anyone grafted into God's tree.
entries.11:19: Someone might argue that branches were broken off just to make room for them. That's true in part, but it's no reason to boast.
entries.11:20: They were removed for lack of faith, and you stand only because of faith—so don't be proud, but be careful. Your place depends on trusting God, not on yourself.
entries.11:21: If God didn't spare the natural branches, he won't spare you either if you turn from him. God's seriousness about faith applies to everyone.
entries.11:22: God is kind, but he is also firm: he was severe with those who fell away and kind to you—if you stay in his kindness; otherwise you too will be cut off. Stay humble and keep trusting him.
entries.11:23: If those branches turn back from unbelief, God is able to graft them in again. No one is beyond God's power to restore.
entries.11:24: If God could graft a wild branch into a good tree, how much more easily can he put the natural branches back where they belong. God's ability to restore his own people is certain.
entries.11:25: Paul wants readers to understand this mystery so they won't become proud: Israel has been hardened only in part, until the full number of non-Jews comes in. God's plan has a timing and a limit.
entries.11:26: In the end all Israel will be saved, as Scripture says a deliverer will come from Zion and remove their wrongdoing. God's promises to his people end in rescue, not ruin.
entries.11:27: This is God's covenant with them: he will take away their sins. Forgiveness is at the heart of God's agreement with his people.
entries.11:28: From the standpoint of the good news they are currently opposed for your sake, but from the standpoint of God's choice they are loved because of the ancestors. God's love for them hasn't been cancelled.
entries.11:29: God doesn't take back his gifts or his call. What he has chosen and promised stays firm.
entries.11:30: You non-Jews were once disobedient but received mercy through their disobedience. God's mercy reached you even through others' failure.
entries.11:31: In the same way, they have now been disobedient so that, through the mercy shown to you, they too may receive mercy. God's mercy to one group is meant to reach the other.
entries.11:32: God allowed everyone to be disobedient so that he could show mercy to everyone. No one earns mercy; all receive it as a gift.
entries.11:33: God's wisdom and knowledge are deeper than we can measure—no one can trace his decisions or figure out his paths. Readers should respond with awe rather than trying to master God.
entries.11:34: No one knows the mind of the Lord or has been his adviser. God doesn't need our input to run the world.
entries.11:35: No one has ever given God something first so that God owed them a repayment. Everything we have came from him in the first place.
entries.11:36: Everything comes from God, exists through him, and is meant for him—so all glory belongs to him forever. The right response to God's greatness is worship.
entries.12:1: Because of all God has done for us, Paul urges believers to offer their whole selves to God—their bodies and daily lives—as a living sacrifice. This means worship is not just singing but giving God your everyday life, which is the right response to his mercy.
entries.12:2: Don't let the world around you shape how you think and act; instead let God change your mind from the inside out. As you do, you'll come to see for yourself what God's good and perfect will is.
entries.12:3: Paul tells each believer not to think too highly of themselves but to be honest and humble about their abilities. God has given each person a measure of faith, so no one should act superior.
entries.12:4: Just as one body has many parts and each part does a different job, so it is among believers.
entries.12:5: Though we are many people, we are joined together as one body in Christ, and each of us belongs to and needs the others.
entries.12:6: God gives different gifts to different people by his grace. Whatever gift you have, use it faithfully and in proportion to the faith God has given you.
entries.12:7: If your gift is serving, throw yourself into serving; if it is teaching, give yourself to teaching. Use your gift wholeheartedly.
entries.12:8: If you are good at encouraging, encourage; if you give, give generously; if you lead, lead diligently; if you show mercy, do it cheerfully. Each gift should be used well.
entries.12:9: Love should be genuine, not fake. Hate what is evil and hold tightly to what is good.
entries.12:10: Treat each other with warm family love and genuinely put others ahead of yourself in showing honor.
entries.12:11: Don't be lazy or half-hearted; serve the Lord with energy and enthusiasm.
entries.12:12: Be hopeful, patient in trouble, constant in prayer. That is a rhythm to keep, not a decision to make once.
entries.12:13: Share what you have with believers who are in need, and be willing to open your home to people.
entries.12:14: When people treat you badly, respond by asking God to bless them rather than cursing them.
entries.12:15: Rejoice with people who are happy and grieve with people who are sad—truly share in their lives.
entries.12:16: Live in harmony with one another, don't act superior, and be willing to associate with ordinary people. Don't think you're the smartest person in the room.
entries.12:17: Never pay back evil for evil. Instead, make sure your conduct is honorable and above reproach in front of everyone.
entries.12:18: Do everything you can on your side to live at peace with everyone.
entries.12:19: Don't take revenge on those who wrong you; leave room for God's judgment, because God says vengeance belongs to him and he will repay.
entries.12:20: If your enemy is hungry or thirsty, feed them and give them something to drink. Doing good to them is like heaping burning coals on their head—it can shame them and change their heart.
entries.12:21: Don't let evil defeat you; instead, defeat evil by doing good.
entries.13:1: God is the one behind all human authority, so Christians should submit to governing rulers. This means respecting the government over you as part of God's order, not rebelling against it.
entries.13:2: Resisting the authorities is resisting what God has set up, and those who do it bring judgment on themselves. The reader should think twice before fighting against the powers that be.
entries.13:3: Rulers are a threat to wrongdoers, not to people doing right. If you want to live without fear of the authorities, do what is good and you will be praised.
entries.13:4: The ruler is God's servant working for your good, but if you do wrong you should be afraid, because he has real power to punish. God uses the government to carry out justice on evildoers.
entries.13:5: Submit to the authorities not just to avoid punishment but because your conscience tells you it is right. The reader should obey out of inner conviction, not only fear.
entries.13:6: This is also why you should pay your taxes, since the authorities are God's servants who keep order. Paying what you owe is part of respecting God's arrangement.
entries.13:7: Give everyone what you owe them: taxes, revenue, respect, and honor to those entitled to it. The reader should not cheat the government or withhold respect from those in authority.
entries.13:8: Owe no one anything except the ongoing debt of loving one another, because whoever loves their neighbor has fulfilled the law. Love is the one debt you should keep paying.
entries.13:9: The commands against adultery, murder, stealing, and coveting are all summed up in loving your neighbor as yourself. If you truly love others, you will not do these things to them.
entries.13:10: Love never harms a neighbor, so love is what makes the law complete. The reader should measure their obedience by whether their actions show real love.
entries.13:11: Wake up, because the time is short and your salvation is closer now than when you first believed. The reader should stop being spiritually sleepy and live with urgency.
entries.13:12: The night of darkness is nearly over and the day is coming, so throw off deeds done in the dark and put on the armor of light. Live as people of the coming day.
entries.13:13: Behave decently as people do in daylight, not in partying, drunkenness, sexual sin, quarreling, or jealousy. The reader should let their conduct match the light they claim to live in.
entries.13:14: Clothe yourself with Jesus Christ and stop planning ways to satisfy your sinful desires. The reader should let Christ shape their life instead of feeding the flesh.
entries.14:1: Welcome people whose faith is still weak instead of arguing with them about their opinions. Your debating could shake their confidence rather than help them.
entries.14:2: One person's faith lets them eat any kind of food, while someone with a weaker faith eats only vegetables. People genuinely differ in what they feel free to do.
entries.14:3: The one who eats freely should not look down on the one who doesn't, and the one who holds back should not condemn the one who eats. God has welcomed both of them.
entries.14:4: You have no right to judge someone else's servant, because their own master decides whether they stand or fall. And they will stand, because the Lord is able to keep them steady.
entries.14:5: One person treats a particular day as special while another treats every day the same. Each person should simply be fully convinced in their own mind.
entries.14:6: Whether someone honors a special day or eats or abstains from food, they do it for the Lord and give God thanks. What matters is that it is done for him.
entries.14:7: None of us lives or dies just for ourselves. Our choices always affect the people around us.
entries.14:8: Whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. That means every part of our life is his, not our own.
entries.14:9: Christ died and rose again so that he could be Lord over both the dead and the living. He has authority over everyone, in life and in death.
entries.14:10: So why do you judge your brother or treat him with contempt? We will all stand before God, who judges everyone.
entries.14:11: Scripture says that every knee will bow to the Lord and every tongue will praise him. In the end, everyone will answer to God.
entries.14:12: Each of us will personally give God an account of our own life. We answer for ourselves, not for each other.
entries.14:13: So stop passing judgment on one another. Instead, decide never to put a stumbling block or obstacle in a brother's way.
entries.14:14: Paul is convinced in the Lord Jesus that no food is unclean in itself. But if someone believes a food is unclean, then for that person it is.
entries.14:15: If your eating of food distresses your brother, you are no longer acting in love. Don't let what you eat destroy someone Christ died for.
entries.14:16: Don't let something you consider good be spoken of as evil by others.
entries.14:17: God's kingdom isn't about food and drink but about right living, peace, and joy given by the Holy Spirit.
entries.14:18: Whoever serves Christ in this way pleases God and earns the respect of people.
entries.14:19: So let's pursue what makes for peace and what builds each other up.
entries.14:20: Don't let food tear down God's work. All foods are clean, but it is wrong for someone if their eating causes another to stumble.
entries.14:21: It is better to give up meat, wine, or anything else than to cause your brother trouble.
entries.14:22: Keep your own convictions about these things between you and God. Blessed is the person who isn't condemned by what they approve of.
entries.14:23: But anyone who eats while doubting is condemned, because they are not acting from faith. And anything that doesn't come from faith is sin.
entries.15:1: People who are strong in faith should help those who are weak instead of just pleasing themselves. If you are strong, use your strength to support others, not just to make your own life easier.
entries.15:2: Each of us should aim to please our neighbor in ways that do them good and help them grow stronger. Think about what builds others up, not just what suits you.
entries.15:3: Christ did not live to please himself; he took on the insults aimed at God. Following him means being willing to put up with trouble for others' sake rather than always choosing comfort.
entries.15:4: The things written long ago in Scripture were written to teach us, so that by patiently enduring and by the encouragement Scripture gives, we can have hope. Read the Bible expecting it to steady you and give you hope.
entries.15:5: Paul prays that God, who gives patience and encouragement, will help them live in harmony with each other, the way Christ wants. Ask God to help you get along with other believers.
entries.15:6: The goal is that together, with one voice, they would honor the God and Father of Jesus Christ. Unity among believers is meant to result in shared worship.
entries.15:7: Accept one another warmly, just as Christ accepted you, and this brings glory to God. Welcome other believers the way Christ welcomed you.
entries.15:8: Christ became a servant to the Jewish people to show that God keeps the promises he made to their ancestors. God's promises are reliable, and Christ came to fulfill them.
entries.15:9: Christ also came so that non-Jewish people could praise God for his mercy, just as Scripture says. God's mercy reaches people of every background, so praise him for it.
entries.15:10: Scripture again invites the Gentiles to rejoice together with God's people. Outsiders are welcomed to share in the joy of belonging to God.
entries.15:11: All the nations are called to praise the Lord. Worship is not for one group only; everyone everywhere is invited to praise him.
entries.15:12: Isaiah foretold that a descendant of Jesse would rise to rule the nations, and the Gentiles would put their hope in him. Jesus is that promised ruler, so your hope can rest in him.
entries.15:13: Hope, joy and peace come from God, not from good circumstances. Hope is meant to overflow.
entries.15:14: Paul says he is confident the believers are full of goodness, well taught, and able to instruct one another. You too can encourage and guide fellow believers.
entries.15:15: Paul writes boldly to remind them of these things because God gave him the job of doing so. It is right to remind each other of what matters, done with grace.
entries.15:16: Paul serves Christ by bringing the good news to non-Jews, so that they become an offering pleasing to God, made holy by the Holy Spirit. God's work in people's lives makes them acceptable to him.
entries.15:17: Paul takes pride in what God has done through Christ Jesus. It is fine to be glad about what God accomplishes, as long as the credit goes to him.
entries.15:18: Paul will only speak of what Christ has done through him to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word and deed. Point to what God has done, not to yourself.
entries.15:19: Paul spread the good news from Jerusalem all the way to Illyricum, backed by signs and wonders and the Spirit's power. God's power works through ordinary people to spread his message.
entries.15:20: Paul made it his aim to preach where Christ had not yet been named, so he would not be building on someone else's foundation. It is good to reach people who have never heard.
entries.15:21: As Scripture says, those who were never told about him will see and understand. People who have never heard the message still need to hear it.
entries.15:22: Because of this work, Paul was often prevented from visiting them. Good plans can be delayed by other important work.
entries.15:23: Now that his work in those regions is finished and he has wanted for years to visit them, he is ready to come. Long-held desires can finally be acted on in God's timing.
entries.15:24: Paul hopes to see them on his way to Spain and be helped on his journey after enjoying their company for a while. Believers can support and encourage each other in their plans.
entries.15:25: Right now Paul is going to Jerusalem to deliver help for the believers there. Serving other believers in practical ways is part of following Christ.
entries.15:26: The churches in Macedonia and Achaia decided to give money to help the poor believers in Jerusalem. Giving to needy believers is a voluntary and good choice.
entries.15:27: They were glad to give because they owe a debt: since Gentiles received spiritual blessings from Jewish believers, it is right to share material help in return. When you receive spiritual good from others, practical generosity is a fitting response.
entries.15:28: After delivering this gift of love, Paul plans to pass through them on his way to Spain. Finish what you have promised, then move on to what is next.
entries.15:29: Paul is sure that when he comes, he will bring the full blessing of Christ. Expect God's blessing when believers meet and share in his work.
entries.15:30: Paul urges them, by Christ and by the Spirit's love, to join him in earnest prayer to God. Praying for others is real partnership in their work.
entries.15:31: He asks them to pray that he will be kept safe from hostile people in Judea and that the relief gift will be welcomed by the believers in Jerusalem. Pray for safety and for good results in ministry.
entries.15:32: He hopes to come to them with joy, by God's will, and to rest with them. Rest and joy with fellow believers are good things to hope for.
entries.15:33: Paul closes by asking that the God of peace be with them all. God's peace is something to ask for and to share with one another.
entries.16:1: Paul is introducing a woman named Phoebe and asking the church to welcome her. He wants them to treat her well because she has served the church faithfully.
entries.16:2: Paul asks the church to receive Phoebe kindly, as fellow believers should, and to help her with whatever she needs. He explains that she has helped many people, including him.
entries.16:3: Paul sends his greetings to Prisca and Aquila, a married couple who worked alongside him to spread the message about Jesus. He wants them to know he remembers their partnership.
entries.16:4: These two risked their lives to protect Paul. He says that not just he but all the non-Jewish churches owe them a debt of gratitude.
entries.16:5: Paul greets the group of believers who meet in Prisca and Aquila's home, and he sends special greetings to Epaenetus, the first person in that region to become a Christian.
entries.16:6: Paul sends greetings to Mary, acknowledging that she worked hard for the believers in Rome. He wants her effort to be recognized.
entries.16:7: Paul greets Andronicus and Junia, fellow Jews who were imprisoned with him and are well respected among the apostles. They became followers of Jesus before Paul did.
entries.16:8: Paul sends a warm greeting to Ampliatus, calling him a dear friend in the Lord. This shows the close personal bond Paul felt with fellow believers.
entries.16:9: Paul greets Urbanus, a co-worker in Christ, and Stachys, whom he calls dear. He values their friendship and their shared work.
entries.16:10: Paul greets Apelles, who has proven his faith, and also sends greetings to the believers connected with Aristobulus's household.
entries.16:11: Paul greets Herodion, a fellow Jew, and the believers in Narcissus's household who follow the Lord. He wants each group to feel remembered.
entries.16:12: Paul greets Tryphaena, Tryphosa, and Persis, women who worked hard for the Lord. He makes a point of honoring their labor.
entries.16:13: Paul greets Rufus, a chosen follower of the Lord, and Rufus's mother, whom Paul affectionately calls his own mother too. This shows the family-like closeness of the early church.
entries.16:14: Paul sends greetings to a group of believers by name, along with the brothers who meet with them. He wants them to know they are remembered.
entries.16:15: Paul greets another group of believers by name and all the saints with them. He makes sure no group is left out of his greetings.
entries.16:16: Paul tells the believers to greet each other warmly with a kiss, a common practice in their culture. He also passes on greetings from all the churches of Christ.
entries.16:17: Paul warns the believers to watch out for people who cause divisions and teach things contrary to what they were taught. He tells them to stay away from such people.
entries.16:18: Such people are not really serving Christ but their own appetites, and they deceive naive people with smooth talk. Paul warns that flattering words can be dangerous.
entries.16:19: Everyone knows how obedient the Roman believers have been, and Paul is glad about that. But he wants them to be wise about what is good and innocent about evil.
entries.16:20: Paul assures them that God, who brings peace, will soon defeat Satan under their feet. He ends with a blessing of grace from Jesus.
entries.16:21: Paul passes on greetings from Timothy, his co-worker, and from Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, who are fellow Jews. They all send their love.
entries.16:22: Tertius, the person who physically wrote down this letter for Paul, adds his own greeting. He wants the believers to know he sends his love in the Lord.
entries.16:23: Gaius, who hosts Paul and the whole church in his home, sends greetings, along with Erastus, the city treasurer, and Quartus. This shows believers from different backgrounds were part of the community.
entries.16:24: This verse repeats the prayer that God's grace would be with all the believers in Rome. It reminds the reader that God's kindness toward us is the foundation of everything, so we can rest in that rather than in our own efforts.
entries.16:25: Paul praises God, who is able to strengthen the believers through the good news about Jesus. This strengthening comes from a plan God kept secret for a very long time.
entries.16:26: That hidden plan has now been revealed through the writings of the prophets, by God's command, so that people of all nations can hear it and come to faith.
entries.16:27: Paul closes by giving glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ forever. This is his final word of praise and trust.
